title: Post-Course Portfolio: Capstone Deployment Exercise
descriptionMarkdown:
# Capstone Deployment Exercise

## Position in the curriculum
This is the closing entry in the post-course portfolio catalog, meant to be done last, applied to a project you have already built rather than a new domain. Its skills (Docker, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, deployment) are exactly the operational skills the final capstone and Phase 5 already required you to demonstrate — this exercise deliberately does not invent a new nineteenth domain to avoid duplicating that content; it asks you to apply it a second time, end to end, to a project of your own choosing.

## Already-proven foundation
Phase 5 and the final capstone already required a non-root container image, external configuration, readiness/liveness probes, and graceful shutdown for the course's own task service. This exercise is where you prove that discipline generalizes, by applying it to a genuinely different application you built yourself.

## Project scope
Choose one completed project from this catalog (the Blog Backend, E-commerce Backend, and Booking/Reservation Core are all good choices; avoid choosing a WebSocket-based project unless you are prepared for the added complexity of a stateful connection surviving a rolling restart). Write a multi-stage `Dockerfile` producing a small, non-root runtime image. Write a `docker-compose.yml` (or equivalent) running the application alongside a real PostgreSQL container, with the database's connection details supplied entirely through environment variables, never baked into the image. Implement (if the chosen project does not already have them) liveness and readiness endpoints, and demonstrate the readiness endpoint correctly reporting not-ready both before the database is reachable and during a simulated graceful shutdown. Document a rollback procedure: if a newly deployed version fails its health checks, what exact steps restore the previous working version.

## Required evidence
- A `docker compose up` from a clean checkout that brings up the application and a fresh PostgreSQL instance, runs pending migrations automatically, and serves traffic, with the exact commands documented in a README.
- Evidence the container image runs as a non-root user (a `docker inspect` or `whoami` check inside the running container).
- A demonstration of the readiness endpoint returning not-ready while the database container is deliberately stopped, and ready again once it is restored.
- A demonstration of graceful shutdown: sending the container a termination signal while a request is in flight, and confirming that request completes before the process exits, per the interruption/cancellation discipline from the concurrency chapter.
- A one-page rollback runbook: exact commands to revert to the previous image tag and confirm the rollback succeeded.

## Review and completion
A reviewer runs your `docker compose up` command on a machine that has never seen this project before, confirms the application comes up correctly against a fresh database with migrations already applied, stops the database container mid-run to confirm the readiness probe reacts correctly, then sends a shutdown signal during an in-flight request and confirms it completes rather than being cut off.
learningObjectives: Build a small, non-root, multi-stage container image for an application built earlier in this course
Run an application and a real database together via Docker Compose with externally supplied configuration
Demonstrate a readiness probe correctly reflecting a genuinely unhealthy dependency, not just a hard-coded true
Demonstrate graceful shutdown completing an in-flight request rather than dropping it
Write and validate a rollback runbook against a deliberately failed deployment
